# Certify reps on the new message with a Forms quiz

*Aug 4, 2026 · svgslid.es blog*

A launch isn't landed until the people selling it can say it. Build a short quiz from the messaging, score it in Sheets, and follow up with whoever missed.

## TL;DR
- Since July 30, Help me create in Google Forms can generate a quiz, with correct answers, from a prompt and files.
- The best wrong answers are your own retired lines. They are plausible because you used to say them.
- Score in Sheets, set a pass mark, and follow up one to one.
- Keep it to ten questions. It checks recall of the message, not product knowledge.

## A message nobody can repeat isn't launched

Product marketing ships the new positioning, the deck, the one-pager. Two weeks later a rep describes the product the old way on a call. The assets changed. The words in people’s mouths didn’t.
A ten-question quiz after the enablement session tells you who has the new message and who needs a second pass. Google Forms has done quizzes for years. What changed is how fast you can build one.

## Route 1: let Gemini draft the quiz

On July 30, Google announced that Help me create in Google Forms now generates quizzes (https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/07/use-gemini-in-google-forms-to-quickly-create-a-new-quiz.html). You describe the quiz in a prompt and point it at files, including PDFs. Gemini drafts the questions, sets quiz settings and marks the correct answers.

    Create a 10-question multiple choice quiz for account executives on our new SSO messaging.
    Use only the approved lines in the attached messaging doc as correct answers.
    Each question gets three wrong answers that sound plausible. Do not invent product facts.

Read every question before you send it. Gemini decides what to ask, and it may test a detail that doesn’t matter. Delete those. Check every correct answer against the messaging doc word for word.
Availability per Google’s post: Business Standard and Plus, Enterprise Standard and Plus, Education Plus.

## Route 2: build it from the messaging sheet

If your messages already live in a sheet, a script gives you exact control. The trick is the wrong answers. Generic distractors are easy to spot. Your **retired lines** are not: they are what the team said last quarter, and they are what a rep will say if the new message didn’t stick.

[Figure: Approved line becomes the correct answer. Retired lines become the wrong ones.]

Add a Question column and up to three Retired columns to the Messages tab. Then, in the sheet, open **Extensions › Apps Script** and paste:

    function buildMessagingQuiz() {
      const sheet = SpreadsheetApp.getActive().getSheetByName('Messages');
      const rows = sheet.getDataRange().getValues().slice(1);   // Key, Question, Approved line, Retired 1, Retired 2, Retired 3
      const form = FormApp.create('Messaging check: ' + new Date().toDateString());
      form.setIsQuiz(true);
      rows.filter(r => r[1] && r[2]).forEach(r => {
        const item = form.addMultipleChoiceItem();
        const options = [item.createChoice(r[2], true)]
          .concat(r.slice(3, 6).filter(String).map(t => item.createChoice(t, false)));
        item.setTitle(r[1]).setChoices(shuffle(options)).setPoints(1).setRequired(true);
      });
      form.setDestination(FormApp.DestinationType.SPREADSHEET, SpreadsheetApp.getActive().getId());
      Logger.log(form.getPublishedUrl());
    }
    
    function shuffle(a) {
      for (let i = a.length - 1; i > 0; i--) { const j = Math.floor(Math.random() * (i + 1)); [a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]]; }
      return a;
    }

Run `buildMessagingQuiz`. It creates a quiz form, one question per row, with the approved line marked correct and the options shuffled, and sends responses to a new tab in the same spreadsheet. The FormApp reference (https://developers.google.com/apps-script/reference/forms) covers every call it uses.

## Score it and follow up

[Figure: Responses land in the sheet with a score. Mockup.]

- **Pass mark:** 8 of 10 is a reasonable start. Add a column: `=IF(C2>=8,"Pass","Follow up")`.
- **Look at the misses by question,** not only by person. If half the team picks the same retired line, the message is the problem, not the reps.
- **Follow up one to one.** A short call beats a public leaderboard.
- **Re-run after a change.** When a line changes, it moves to a Retired column and becomes a wrong answer in the next quiz.

## What we have tested

- **Not yet run by us:** the script above. It is written against the FormApp reference. Run it on a copy of your sheet first.
- **Not yet tried by us:** quiz generation with Help me create. Our account did not have it when we wrote this.

The screens in this post are mockups, not captures of Google’s products. Google Slides, Google Sheets, Google Docs, Google Forms, Google Meet, Google Chat, Google Drive, Gemini and Google Workspace are trademarks of Google LLC.

# Localize a one-pager without breaking the layout

*Jul 31, 2026 · svgslid.es blog*

Translations run long. Give every slot a budget per language, draft in Sheets, and catch the overflow before it reaches the page.

## TL;DR
- Translated copy is a layout problem first. German and French lines often run longer than English; Japanese is shorter in characters but wider per character.
- Keep one row per slot in Sheets and one column per language, each with its own character budget.
- Draft with the Sheets AI function. Fill with Gemini now works in 11 more languages. A native speaker approves.
- Flag anything over budget in the sheet. Fix length there, never by shrinking type on the page.

## The page breaks before the translation does

A one-pager is built around its English copy. The headline box is sized for eight words. The three benefit columns are sized for two short lines each. Then the German version arrives and every box overflows.
You can fix it slide by slide, file by file, every launch. Or you can treat length as data and catch it before it reaches a page. The second way takes one sheet.

## One row per slot, one column per language

Every text box on the page is a slot with a key: `headline`, `subhead`, `benefit_1_title`. The sheet has one row per key. Each language gets a copy column and a budget column.

[Figure: One row per slot. The German headline is 11 characters over. Mockup.]

- **Key:** the slot name. It never changes between languages.
- **Source line:** the approved English line.
- **Budget per language:** the most characters that slot can hold in that language, at that size, in that font. Set it by filling the box until it looks full, then counting.
- **Fits:** `=IF(LEN(D2)<=E2,"OK","Over by "&(LEN(D2)-E2))`

Budgets differ by language for two reasons. Some languages need more letters to say the same thing. And a character count is a stand-in for width: a Japanese character takes far more room than a Latin *i*. Measure each language in its own font.

## Draft the translation in the sheet

Google announced on July 7 that Fill with Gemini in Sheets works in 11 more languages (https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/07/fill-with-gemini-in-sheets-now-available-in-11-additional-languages.html). Fill with Gemini runs on the AI function (https://support.google.com/docs/answer/15877199), so you can write the budget into the prompt:

    =AI("Translate this product marketing line into German. Keep it under "&E2&" characters. Plain, specific, no exclamation marks.", B2)

Three rules keep this safe:

- **A draft is a draft.** A native speaker who knows the product approves every line. Machine drafts miss product terms and register.
- **Keep a glossary tab.** Product names, feature names and terms you never translate. Paste the relevant terms into the prompt.
- **Keep draft and approved separate.** A formula can recalculate. An approved line must not. Paste approved lines as values.

## Catch overflow in the sheet, not on the page

[Figure: One headline, four languages, one box. Budgets are set per language.]

When a line is over budget, shorten the line. Do not shrink the font for one language. A German headline set smaller than the English one breaks the type system you built for every other asset, and readers notice.
Some fixes that work:

- **Write a shorter source line.** If three languages run over, the English line is too long for the layout.
- **Allow a two-line headline** in the layout, and budget for two lines in every language.
- **Split long compounds** with your translator, or choose a shorter term from the glossary.

## Fonts per language

Your brand font may not cover every script. Overpass, our headline font, has no Japanese glyphs. Pick a fallback per language and record it in the sheet, so everyone uses the same one. Google Fonts has Noto families for most scripts. Re-measure budgets in the fallback font.
Check letter spacing too. A tracked-out all-caps eyebrow in English can look wrong in a script with no capitals. Set tracking per language.

## One file per language

- Make a copy of the finished English file for each language. Keep page size, layout and slot names identical.
- Name files the same way: `One-pager - Relay - de-DE`.
- Paste approved lines slot by slot. If you tag text boxes with their key in the alt text title, a script can do this for every language at once.
- Look at every page after the copy lands. A count is an estimate; line breaks still surprise.

Logos and icons should not change between languages. Keep them as vectors so one file serves every version: see how to add a logo to Google Slides as an editable SVG (https://svgslid.es/guides/svg-logos-icons-google-slides).

## What we have tested

- **Checked in Sheets:** the LEN-based fit formula.
- **Not checked by us:** translation quality from the AI function in each of the 11 new languages. Google’s post lists them; treat every draft as a draft.

*Update, Nov 2026:* the slot-and-sync approach mentioned above is now written up in full in Update Google Slides collateral from one messaging sheet with Gemini (https://svgslid.es/blog/google-slides-collateral-messaging-sheet-gemini).

# About SVG to Slides

SVG to Slides turns SVG files into native, editable shapes inside Google Slides. Every path becomes its own shape: select it, recolour it with the standard fill picker, resize it without losing quality.

- Three ways in: Chrome extension (https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/svg-to-slides/bdhhnakellmdnbgbdokiojipaebdeioi), web uploader (https://svgslid.es/convert), Google Slides add-on (https://svgslid.es/addon).
- The extension asks for no access to your Google account.
- Free forever. Every feature, no daily cap, no account, no Pro tier.

## Why it exists
Slides has no way to import an SVG; pasted SVGs flatten into images. Where there should be crisp icons and logos, there are crunchy PNGs.

## How it works
SVG to Slides writes Google Slides' own clipboard shape format from your SVG's paths. You paste, and Slides treats the result as native shapes. The extension converts inside your browser.

## Who builds it
Joe Gelman, independently. Contact: joe@glmn.co
